claims.text: Five-or-more-element near-equiatomic nanoparticles have high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy maintains a single-phase solid solution up to 1923 K.
Configurational entropy counteracts enthalpy-driven phase segregation.
Short-range order helps prevent large-scale phase segregation.
High mixing entropy helps prevent large-scale phase segregation.
Elevated configurational entropy offsets the thermodynamic driving force for elemental demixing.
The reduction in thermodynamic driving force kinetically inhibits phase transformation.
The proposed mechanism preserves a single-phase solid solution throughout 473–1923 K.
Heating within 473–1923 K will produce minimal compositional segregation relative to the initial state.
X-ray diffraction will retain a pattern consistent with a single phase after heating.
Elemental maps will remain spatially uniform across the nanoparticle population after heating.
Lower-entropy or fewer-element alloys undergo segregation and possible phase transformations at elevated temperatures.
Significant deviations from equimolar composition can overcome entropic stabilization and cause segregation.
Extreme thermal cycling can overcome entropic stabilization and cause segregation.
Reactions with contaminants can overcome entropic stabilization and cause segregation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism assert preservation through 1923 K and throughout the full operational window, while the uncertainty field says the precise temperature limits remain undetermined.
